lead: At a post-tensioned anchorage, a force of hundreds or thousands of kilonewtons enters the concrete through a steel plate a few hundred millimetres square. The force cannot stay concentrated; within a length about equal to the depth of the member it spreads out until the stress is the ordinary P/A ± Pe/Z of the whole section. The region where it spreads is the end block or anchorage zone. The spreading pulls the concrete apart sideways, so every end block needs bearing area and transverse steel, and its design is a standard exam question.
prereq: You need post-tensioning anchorages and the force after jacking from losses of prestress.

blocks.text: Follow the lines of compression from a small plate on the end face. They start bunched under the plate, fan out, and become parallel and evenly spaced about one end-block depth in from the face. Where the lines bend outward, their change of direction needs a tensile force at right angles to them, across the member: this is bursting tension. It is zero at the face, peaks at roughly 0.3 to 0.5 of the block depth behind it, and dies away by the end of the zone. The stress pattern was worked out by Magnel, Guyon and Rowe; a strut-and-tie model shows the same thing as two inclined struts held together by a transverse tie.

Close to the loaded face, around the edges of the plate and in the corners between widely spaced anchorages, there is a second, local tension called spalling tension. It is caused by the concrete next to the plate being dragged along by the deformation under it. It can break off the corners and cover, so a light mesh is placed right behind the face. Some books call the small region just under the plate the primary (local) zone and the larger spreading region the secondary (general) zone.

The first check is that the concrete under the plate does not crush. The concrete round the loaded area confines it, so the permitted bearing stress rises with the ratio of the area available for spreading to the loaded area. IS 1343 limits it to:

blocks.where: f<sub>ci</sub> is the cube strength at transfer in N/mm²; A<sub>pun</sub> is the punching area, the contact area of the anchorage plate in mm²; A<sub>br</sub> is the bearing area, the largest area of the end face that is similar to and concentric with A<sub>pun</sub>, in mm². The actual stress is P<sub>k</sub>/A<sub>pun</sub>, where P<sub>k</sub> is the jacking force in N.

blocks.text: If the bearing stress is too high, enlarge the plate, use a stronger concrete at transfer, or spread the anchorages; stirrups do not cure a bearing failure.

IS 1343 gives the total bursting force across each principal direction of a square end block loaded by a square plate, as a fraction of P<sub>k</sub> depending on the ratio of plate size 2y<sub>po</sub> to block size 2y<sub>o</sub> in that direction:

The table is the straight line F<sub>bst</sub>/P<sub>k</sub> = 0.32 − 0.3(2y<sub>po</sub>/2y<sub>o</sub>). A rectangular end block is checked in each direction separately, with the plate and block sizes in that direction. The steel is designed at 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>:

blocks.where: F<sub>bst</sub> in N and f<sub>y</sub> in N/mm² give A<sub>st</sub> in mm². Use closed links, mesh or a spiral round each anchorage.

items: Find F<sub>bst</sub> in both directions from the table.
Provide closed links or mesh for the larger demand in each direction, spread through the bursting zone, from close behind the plate to about one end-block depth in.
Add a surface mesh just behind the face for spalling, and lap the links with the beam stirrups beyond the zone.

examples.question: A post-tensioned beam has an end block 400 mm wide and 500 mm deep. A single tendon with jacking force 1000 kN is anchored at the centre through a 200 mm × 200 mm plate. f<sub>ci</sub> = 40 N/mm² and Fe 415 links are used. Check the bearing stress and design the bursting reinforcement.
steps: Bearing: A<sub>pun</sub> = 200 × 200 = 40,000 mm². The largest concentric square on a 400 mm wide face is 400 × 400, so A<sub>br</sub> = 160,000 mm²; √(A<sub>br</sub>/A<sub>pun</sub>) = 2.
Permitted f<sub>b</sub> = 0.48 × 40 × 2 = 38.4, but not more than 0.8 × 40 = 32 N/mm², so f<sub>b</sub> = 32 N/mm². Actual = 1,000,000/40,000 = 25 N/mm² ≤ 32: safe.
Across the width (horizontal tension): 2y<sub>po</sub>/2y<sub>o</sub> = 200/400 = 0.5; F<sub>bst</sub>/P<sub>k</sub> = 0.32 − 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.17; F<sub>bst</sub> = 170 kN.
Over the depth (vertical tension): 200/500 = 0.4; F<sub>bst</sub>/P<sub>k</sub> = 0.32 − 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.2; F<sub>bst</sub> = 200 kN.
Steel at 0.87 × 415 = 361.05 N/mm²: horizontal legs 170,000/361.05 = 471 mm²; vertical legs 200,000/361.05 = 554 mm².
A closed 10 mm link gives two legs in each direction, 157 mm². Vertical demand 554/157 = 3.53 → 4 links (628 mm²), which also covers the 471 mm² horizontal demand.
Place the 4 links at 140 mm centres, at 50, 190, 330 and 470 mm behind the face, so they span the 500 mm bursting zone, plus a 6 mm mesh at 75 mm centres just behind the face for spalling.
examples.answer: Bearing 25 N/mm² against 32 N/mm² permitted. Bursting forces 200 kN (vertical) and 170 kN (horizontal) need 554 and 471 mm²; four 10 mm closed links (628 mm² each way) spread through the first 500 mm satisfy both.

traps: Designing end-block steel as flexural steel. It resists transverse splitting; there is no lever arm.
Using the end-block depth for the ratio in the other direction. Plate and block sizes must be taken in the same direction, and both directions checked.
Mixing units in the bearing check: P in kN over area in mm² is not N/mm²; convert to N.
Trying to fix a bearing failure with more links. Enlarge the plate or the concrete strength.
Forgetting the spalling mesh at the face; the bursting links sit deeper in the block.

quiz.q: Define bursting tension and spalling tension.
quiz.a: Bursting tension: transverse tension inside the end block, behind the plate, caused by the spreading of the anchorage force. Spalling tension: local tension near the loaded face around the plate edges and between anchorages.

quiz.q: Why does a concentrated anchorage force create transverse tension?
quiz.a: The compression lines fan out from the small plate to the full section. Where they change direction, equilibrium needs a force at right angles to them, which is tension across the member.

quiz.q: Why is the end-block problem mainly a post-tensioning problem?
quiz.a: In pre-tensioning the force enters gradually by bond over the transmission length, so it is not concentrated at a plate; only light links are needed near the end.

quiz.q: P<sub>k</sub> = 800 kN acts through a 150 mm × 150 mm plate on a 300 mm × 300 mm end block. Find F<sub>bst</sub>.
quiz.a: Ratio 150/300 = 0.5; F<sub>bst</sub>/P<sub>k</sub> = 0.17; F<sub>bst</sub> = 0.17 × 800 = 136 kN in each direction.

quiz.q: For that end block, find the links needed with Fe 415 and the bearing stress for f<sub>ci</sub> = 35 N/mm².
quiz.a: A<sub>st</sub> = 136,000/361.05 = 377 mm²: three 10 mm closed links (471 mm²) each way. Bearing: actual 800,000/22,500 = 35.6 N/mm²; permitted 0.48 × 35 × √(90,000/22,500) = 33.6, capped at 0.8 × 35 = 28 N/mm². Since 35.6 > 28, the plate is too small: a 170 mm plate (27.7 N/mm²) would do.

quiz.q: A designer doubles the plate width for the same force. What happens to the bearing stress and the bursting force?
quiz.a: The bearing stress falls to a quarter for a square plate, but the permitted stress also falls because A<sub>br</sub>/A<sub>pun</sub> drops. The ratio 2y<sub>po</sub>/2y<sub>o</sub> rises, so F<sub>bst</sub> falls; a plate covering the whole face would need no bursting steel, but would leave no room for cover.

beyond: Not for the exam. Where several large tendons anchor close together, as in bridge girders and segmental box decks, designers use strut-and-tie models and three-dimensional finite element analysis, and suppliers sell anchorages with spiral reinforcement tested as a unit. Search for strut-and-tie anchorage zone design and special anchorage devices.
